taxonomy.subtopic: Dystrophin-glycoprotein complex linkage between actin and extracellular matrix

questions.stem_html: A 4-year-old boy has difficulty running, uses his hands to push on his thighs when rising from the floor, and has enlarged calves. Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated. A maternal uncle died of respiratory failure in his twenties. The accompanying schematic shows a missing protein at the muscle-cell membrane. Loss of this protein most directly disrupts which normal function?

options.text_html: Mechanical linkage of the intracellular actin cytoskeleton to a transmembrane complex connected with extracellular matrix
Calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum through the ryanodine receptor
ATP-dependent reuptake of calcium into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Transmission of acetylcholine signals through postsynaptic nicotinic receptors
Assembly of thick filaments from myosin heavy chains

questions.explanation_html: Dystrophin binds intracellular actin and participates in the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex, which connects the cytoskeleton to membrane proteins and the extracellular matrix. Absence of functional dystrophin makes the sarcolemma mechanically fragile during contraction, promoting calcium entry, myofiber necrosis, elevated creatine kinase and progressive replacement by fat and connective tissue.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: The ryanodine receptor releases calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum; its dysfunction causes disorders such as malignant hyperthermia, not the classic X-linked dystrophinopathy.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: SERCA pumps return calcium to the sarcoplasmic reticulum and permit relaxation; this pump is not the missing membrane-linkage protein in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors mediate neuromuscular transmission and are targeted in myasthenia gravis, which does not cause calf pseudohypertrophy or very high creatine kinase.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Myosin forms the thick filament and generates force, but dystrophin is a membrane-associated cytoskeletal linker rather than a contractile filament protein.

questions.educational_objective: Dystrophin stabilizes skeletal muscle by linking actin to the dystrophin-associated membrane complex and extracellular matrix; its absence causes contraction-induced sarcolemmal injury.
